lesson.title: The Right-Hand Limit: Closing In From Above
lesson.summary: The right-hand limit mirrors the left-hand limit from the opposite direction, and comparing the two at the same point on the floor function versus on a smooth parabola shows exactly when a graph has a real jump.
lesson.body:
The right-hand limit mirrors the left-hand limit exactly, but from the opposite direction: it restricts x to values strictly greater than a, written lim(x to a+) f(x), and asks what the function's outputs do as those larger inputs shrink down toward a. The raised plus mark signals "approach from above, using only inputs bigger than a," the counterpart to the minus mark's "from below."

Return to the same floor function used for the left-hand limit, f(x) = floor(x), and this time compute lim(x to 2+) floor(x). Restrict attention to inputs strictly greater than 2, closing in on 2 from that side: x = 2.1 gives floor(2.1) = 2. x = 2.01 gives floor(2.01) = 2. x = 2.001 gives floor(2.001) = 2. In fact, for every x satisfying 2 <= x < 3, floor(x) = 2 exactly. So as x approaches 2 from the right, the output holds steady at 2 the entire time once x is within that stretch, and lim(x to 2+) floor(x) = 2.

The sqrt(x) example from the one-sided limit discussion is really a right-hand limit in disguise, and it is worth revisiting directly. Since sqrt(x) is only defined for x >= 0, the only limit that makes sense at a = 0 is the right-hand one: lim(x to 0+) sqrt(x). Testing values confirms this. x = 0.01 gives sqrt(0.01) = 0.1. x = 0.0001 gives sqrt(0.0001) = 0.01. As x shrinks toward 0 through positive values, sqrt(x) shrinks toward 0 as well, so lim(x to 0+) sqrt(x) = 0, matching sqrt(0) = 0 exactly, which makes sense since sqrt(x) has no jump or hole anywhere on its domain.

Compare this to the left-hand result from the previous section: lim(x to 2-) floor(x) = 1, while lim(x to 2+) floor(x) = 2. The two one-sided limits at the very same point disagree, 1 versus 2, which reflects the real jump in the floor function's graph right at x = 2: approaching from below, the function is stuck at 1; approaching from above, it has already jumped to 2. Both computations are individually correct; they are simply describing two different neighborhoods of the same point.

It's worth also checking a case where the two sides agree, to see that disagreement is not automatic. For f(x) = x^2 at a = 2: from the right, x = 2.1 gives f(2.1) = 4.41, x = 2.01 gives 4.0401, both closing in on 4. From the left, x = 1.9 gives f(1.9) = 3.61, x = 1.99 gives 3.9601, also closing in on 4. Here lim(x to 2-) x^2 = lim(x to 2+) x^2 = 4: the smooth, unbroken graph of x^2 has no jump at x = 2, so both directions of approach land on the same value.

The floor-function jump and the parabola's agreement together preview the exact question the next section answers directly: when do the left-hand and right-hand limits have to match for the plain, unrestricted limit to make sense at all? And the sqrt(x) case shows a third possibility worth keeping in mind: sometimes only one side is even available to check, because the function's domain rules the other side out entirely.
